meta.title: Checkpoint: Where the Roots Are
meta.summary: The letter names the form, the five windows tile the neck, and every C in the first twelve frets has a home.

prompt.text: You barre the C form with the barre at fret 5, so the root that sat on string 5, fret 3 in the open chord now sits on string 5, fret 8. Which chord are you playing?

explanation.text: . The letter in CAGED names the shape of the arrangement — what those fingers would spell sitting at the nut — never the chord that comes out. Answering
is the misconception this chapter exists to kill; answering
reads the barre fret as the root instead of the root's own fret.

prompt.text: Why do players take fragments of the C form rather than barring it whole?

spans.text: while the other fingers have to reach out to
The C form only holds two roots, so the strings without one have to be muted.
The C form lives at the nut, and a form at the nut cannot be barred at all.
The C form crosses the B string, and a barre across the B string buzzes.

explanation.text: It is a reach problem, nothing more. Fragments — the top four strings, or the low root with its neighbours on strings 5, 4 and 3 — are how this form actually gets played, and that is the normal case rather than a concession. The B string does bend the C form's roots out of a clean diagonal, but that is a fact about pitch, not about what your hand can hold.

prompt.text: roots inside their window? Select every one that does.

explanation.text: The G form holds roots on strings 6, 3 and 1; the E form holds them on strings 6, 4 and 1. The C form (5 and 2), the A form (5 and 3) and the D form (4 and 2) hold two each. The count is not trivia: three roots spanning all six strings is what makes the G form the one for
where a chord lives, and the E form's three are what you find from a single note on the low E string.

prompt.text: You have found a root on string 6, fret 8. Using the E form's root map — and without counting up from the nut — where are its other two roots?

The B string is thinner, so it sounds sharp and needs an extra fret to compensate.

prompt.text: in the first five frets. There are three of them, and between them they belong to the C, A and G forms.

explanation.text: String 2 fret 1 and string 5 fret 3 are the C form's pair; string 5 fret 3 and string 3 fret 5 are the A form's; and string 3 fret 5 is also the G form's middle root. Three positions, three forms, and two of the three positions shared — the overlap in miniature.

prompt.text: s in the first twelve frets, and the five forms between them account for all six. What does that tell you about the forms?

spans.text: Most of those roots sit inside two forms at once, so the windows share their edges.
Each form holds its own separate roots, so learning five forms is five times the work.
Only one form is really needed; the other four are alternative fingerings of it.
The forms never touch, which is why you have to jump between them.

explanation.text: Five of the six belong to two forms each — only string 2, fret 1 sits in one form alone, because there is no form below the C form to share it with. The five forms are not five sets of different notes; they are five overlapping views of one set of six. That overlap is what makes the neck continuous instead of five islands.

prompt.text: You are at the D form, barre at fret 10, and you keep climbing. What is the next window up the neck?

spans.text: Nothing — the D form is the last of the five.
The E form again, since it is the most-used barre on the instrument.
The G form, because the order runs backwards above the twelfth fret.

explanation.text: is cyclic, not a list with an end. Fret 12 is where the nut's own pattern comes back around, so the ladder wraps and the C form starts over there — and it reads the same way going down, where below any form sits the one before it in the order.
